opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to the difference between solving a problem and deciding which problem is worth solving.

AI is getting very good at the first part. If you give a model a well-defined task with a clear objective, like writing this function, passing these tests, or optimizing this metric, it can increasingly do it as well as or better than people. A lot of my thinking about agents is really about this: once the environment and the reward are clear, progress becomes almost inevitable.

But product management lives mostly in the part *before* things are well-defined. You're asking: what do people actually want? What do they say they want versus what they'll really use? What's the right trade-off between ten things that all seem important? That isn't a task with a clean reward signal. The "reward" is human preference, and human preference is messy, contextual, and changes over time. Often people don't know it themselves until they see something.

Humans have a natural advantage there, not because we're smarter, but because we *are* the users. You have taste and lived experience. You feel the friction when a product is annoying. You can sit with a user, notice what they hesitate on, and understand the social and emotional context around it. That kind of grounding is very hard to get from data alone.

There's also a deeper point. As AI handles more of the execution, the bottleneck shifts. If building becomes cheap, then *what to build* becomes the most valuable question. So in a sense, product thinking becomes more important, not less. Everyone becomes a bit of a product manager, defining goals, judging outputs, and deciding direction, while the AI does more of the doing.

I wouldn't say it's permanently safe. Models will get better at modeling human preferences too. But I think it's one of the last places to be fully automated, because it's where the objective function itself gets defined, and that's fundamentally about humans.

r001.rationale: The response says people may not know what they want until they see a product, but does not state that product quality becomes knowable only through users’ reactions after they have used it.

r002.rationale: It says product management lacks a clean reward signal because human preferences are messy, contextual, and change over time.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the way to look at it is through the lens of what AI is actually good at versus where the real bottleneck is. In my own work, and in a lot of the agent research I've done, the pattern that keeps showing up is that the models are increasingly capable of execution. If you give a model a well-defined task with a clear objective, a clear environment, and a way to check whether it succeeded, it will get better and better at that, and probably faster than most people expect. Coding is the obvious example. Once you have the spec, once you have tests, once the goal is crisp, the agent can just iterate.

But product management is almost the opposite of that. The hard part of a PM's job is not execution. It's figuring out what the objective should be in the first place. It's deciding what to build, for whom, why now, and what tradeoffs you're willing to make. And those questions don't come with a reward signal. There's no test suite that tells you whether you picked the right problem. You find out six months or a year later, and even then the feedback is noisy, confounded by a hundred other things. So from a reinforcement learning perspective, this is the exact regime where it's very hard to train a model to be good, because the environment is ambiguous and the feedback is sparse and delayed.

There's a second piece that I think gets underestimated, which is that a lot of product judgment is really about understanding people. Understanding what users actually want, which is often not what they say. Understanding what your team can realistically build, what the organization's politics are, what the market will tolerate. That knowledge is tacit and relational. It lives in conversations, in taste, in having been burned before. AI can help you simulate some of this, it can summarize feedback, it can generate options, but the act of deciding, of taking responsibility for a bet when the data doesn't tell you the answer, that still feels deeply human to me.

So I'd put it this way. As AI makes execution cheap, the scarce thing becomes deciding what to execute. The value shifts upstream, toward problem definition, toward taste, toward understanding the humans on both sides of the product. And that's essentially what good product management is. It's not that AI can't contribute there, it's that the PM role is the one that's most about the parts AI is structurally weakest at. If anything, I think the best engineers in the next few years will start to look more like PMs, because the thing they need to be good at is no longer writing the code, it's knowing what's worth building.

r001.rationale: The response says product decisions are evaluated later through noisy, delayed feedback, but does not clearly state that product quality becomes knowable through users’ reactions after the product is built and used.

r002.rationale: It says there is no reward signal or test suite for choosing the right problem, and identifies sparse, delayed feedback as why training a model to make good product decisions is difficult.

astra-6.text:
I think product management is interesting because it’s about deciding what problem is worth solving, not just solving a problem once it’s clearly specified. As AI gets better at implementation, that distinction becomes more important. You can build many more things, but you still have to decide which things people actually need and what success should look like.

And those questions are often ambiguous. Users may not be able to articulate what they want. You have to understand their context, make tradeoffs, and learn from how they respond to something you put in front of them. Humans participate in that social world, so they have useful context for making those judgments.

I wouldn’t say product management is permanently protected from automation. AI can help with those decisions too. But if execution becomes much cheaper, the relative value of choosing the right direction can increase. That’s the part I think humans may continue to do relatively well.

r001.rationale: The response says product managers learn from users’ reactions to something they put in front of them, but does not state that product quality becomes knowable only after the product is built and used.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss training AI or a lack of a clear reward signal for product quality.

sol-6.1.text:
I think product management is interesting because it involves deciding what problem is worth solving, not just figuring out how to solve a problem that’s already specified. AI is getting very good at the second part. But in a real product, the objective is often unclear. You have to talk to users, understand what they actually need, and decide which tradeoffs you’re willing to make.

And users themselves may not be able to tell you exactly what they want. They can react to something you build, but turning those reactions into a direction requires judgment. As implementation becomes cheaper, that judgment could become more valuable: you can build many things, so which one should you build?

That doesn’t mean AI can’t do product management. It can certainly help with research, prototypes, and analyzing feedback. But humans may continue to have an advantage in setting the direction, because we’re part of the human context the product is meant to serve.

r001.rationale: The response says users can react to something built, but does not state that product quality becomes knowable only after users have built and used it.

r002.rationale: It discusses unclear objectives and human judgment, but does not attribute AI training difficulty to the lack of a clear reward signal for product quality.
